Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]), let $S$ be a finite set with $n:=|S|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and let $a:S\to M$. Choose a bijection $\phi:n\to S$ and define

$$\sum_{s\in S}a_s:=a_{\phi(0)}+a_{\phi(1)}+\cdots+a_{\phi(n-1)},$$

where the right side is the finite monoid product of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] written additively. In particular, the sum over the empty set is $0$.

This value is independent of the enumeration. If $\psi:n\to S$ is another bijection, then $\phi^{-1}\circ\psi$ is a permutation of $n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and generalised commutativity gives

$$\sum_{k<n}a_{\psi(k)}=\sum_{k<n}a_{\phi(k)}$$

([[thm-generalised-associativity]]). Thus the displayed notation names one element of $M$ and does not select a preferred enumeration.

When $M$ is the additive monoid of $\mathbb R$ or of $\mathbb N$, this definition agrees with [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]: both enumerate $S$, apply the same finite recursion with identity $0$, and are independent of the enumeration.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Fix $z\in\mathbb C$. Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set $\mathbb C$, the
initial value $1$, and the function $w\mapsto wz$. This defines the natural
powers uniquely by
$$ z^0=1,\qquad z^{n+1}=z^nz\quad(n\in\mathbb N). $$

Let $\jmath\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ be the embedding of
[[lem-nat-embeds-int]]. For an integer $r\ge0$, that lemma gives a unique
$n\in\mathbb N$ with $r=\jmath(n)$; define $z^r:=z^n$. If $r<0$ and $z\ne0$,
there is a unique $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $-r=\jmath(n)$; define
$$ z^r:=(z^n)^{-1}. $$
The inverse exists because $\mathbb C$ is a field by
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]. Thus nonnegative integer powers are
defined for every $z$, while negative integer powers are defined exactly when
$z\ne0$; in particular $0^0=1$ and no negative power of $0$ is defined. The
integer and its unique natural representative are never conflated.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

derivations.claim: At $n=0$, the sum is empty, so $(1-z)S_0(z)=0=1-z^0$ by [F1] and [F2].
Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and assume $(1-z)S_n(z)=1-z^n$; this is the induction hypothesis.

By [F1] and [F2], $(1-z)S_{n+1}=(1-z)S_n+(1-z)z^n=(1-z^n)+(z^n-z^{n+1})=1-z^{n+1}$, using distributivity in [F3] and the induction hypothesis [step 1.2]. Thus [F5] proves $(1-z)S_n(z)=1-z^n$ for every $n$.

If $z=1$, every summand is $1$, so [F1] gives $S_0(1)=0$ and $S_{n+1}(1)=S_n(1)+1$. At $n=0$, this equals $\iota_{\mathbb C}(0)=0$ by [F4]; if $S_n(1)=\iota_{\mathbb C}(n)$, the two successor recursions give $S_{n+1}(1)=S_n(1)+1=\iota_{\mathbb C}(n)+1=\iota_{\mathbb C}(n+1)$. Induction [F5] proves $S_n(1)=\iota_{\mathbb C}(n)$ for every $n$. If $z\ne1$, then $1-z\ne0$, so divide the identity from step 2.1 by $1-z$ in the field [F3] to obtain $S_n(z)=(1-z^n)/(1-z)$.

In the QPE specialization, repeated use of [F6] and the power recursion [F2] gives $z^Q=\exp(2\pi iQ(\theta-y/Q))=\exp(2\pi i(Q\theta-y))$. Since $y\in\mathbb Z$, [F6] gives $\exp(-2\pi iy)=1$, hence $z^Q=\exp(2\pi iQ\theta)$. The same kernel statement gives $z=1$ exactly when $2\pi i(\theta-y/Q)\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$, equivalently $\theta-y/Q\in\mathbb Z$, or $Q\theta-y\in Q\mathbb Z$.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For all real $u,v$,

$$|\sin u-\sin v|\le|u-v|,$$

and

$$|\cos u-\cos v|\le|u-v|.$$

Thus sine and cosine are Lipschitz functions on $\mathbb R$, each with
Lipschitz constant $1$.

derivations.claim: Define $g(t)=\sin t-2t/\pi$ on $[0,\pi/2]$. By [F1], [F3], and [F4], $g(0)=g(\pi/2)=0$ and $g'(t)=\cos t-2/\pi$ on the interior.
By [F2], $g'$ is nonincreasing: if $s<t$, then $\cos s\ge\cos t$, so $g'(s)\ge g'(t)$.

Fix $t\in(0,\pi/2)$. Apply [F5] on $[0,t]$ and $[t,\pi/2]$ to obtain $a\in(0,t)$ and $b\in(t,\pi/2)$ with $g(t)=t g'(a)$ and $-g(t)=(\pi/2-t)g'(b)$. Since $a<b$, step 2.1 gives $g'(a)\ge g'(b)$. Dividing by the positive numbers $t$ and $\pi/2-t$, then multiplying by their product, gives $g(t)\pi/2\ge0$; as $\pi>0$, $g(t)\ge0$.
If $0<u<1/2$, take $t=\pi u\in(0,\pi/2)$ in step 3.1 to get $\sin(\pi u)\ge2u$. At $u=0$ and $u=1/2$, the same inequality is equality by [F1].
For $v\ge0$, [F6] and $\sin0=0$ give $\sin v=\sin v-\sin0\le|\sin v-\sin0|\le v$. Thus both stated inequalities hold.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $U:H\to H$ a unitary, and $\psi\in H$ a unit vector with a promised phase $\theta\in[0,1)$ such that
$$U\psi=\exp(2\pi i\theta)\psi.$$
For an integer $m\ge1$, let $Q=2^m$. The phase register is $(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}$ with ordered computational basis indexed big-endian by
$x=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}b_k2^{m-1-k}$, where $b_k\in\{0,1\}$ ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]).
Thus the wire of weight $2^j$ is $q_{m-1-j}$.

There are distinct forward-access options:

1. **Controlled-power access.** The model explicitly supplies one controlled $U^{2^j}$ operation for each $j=0,\ldots,m-1$. Each use is counted as one controlled-power query; an implementation's ordinary gate cost is recorded separately.
2. **Single controlled-unitary access.** The model supplies calls to $C(U)=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,U)$ in the control-first order of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. A controlled $U^{2^j}$ may be implemented by $2^j$ sequential calls to $C(U)$; those calls are charged individually.

Optional **controlled inverse-power access** is a separate capability that explicitly supplies $C(U^{-2^j})$ for each required $j$. It is not implied by either forward option. It is needed only by a consuming procedure that reverses the controlled-power portion of a coherent QPE prefix. Reversing the inverse-QFT gate list does not use $U^{-1}$.

The finite ordered-register, gate, and measurement interpretations are those of [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]]. The definition is an access-model promise: it does not assert that the supplied controlled powers have an efficient construction or that $\theta$ has an exact $m$-bit expansion.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

**Input.** An integer $m\ge1$; an $m$-qubit phase register; a finite-dimensional system register $H$; a unitary $U:H\to H$; a unit eigenvector $\psi$ with promised phase $\theta\in[0,1)$; and one of the forward access capabilities in [[def-qa-eigenphase-estimation-model]].

**Output.** A classical label $y\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$ and its phase estimate $y/Q$, where $Q=2^m$.

**Instructions.**

1. Initialize the phase register in $|0^m\rangle$ and the system register in $\psi$.
2. Apply the Hadamard $H=(X+Z)/\sqrt2$ of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] to each phase wire. This prepares $Q^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{Q-1}|x\rangle\otimes\psi$ in the declared big-endian order.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,m-1$, apply the supplied controlled $U^{2^j}$ to control wire $q_{m-1-j}$ and the system. Under single controlled-unitary access, implement that operation with $2^j$ sequential calls to $C(U)$, as specified by the access model.
4. Apply the inverse of the positive-sign exact binary QFT circuit of [[def-qa-cyclic-quantum-fourier-transform]] and [[thm-qa-exact-binary-qft-circuit-correct]]. Construct it by reversing the chronological gate list and replacing each gate by its adjoint, including the final swaps and negating controlled-phase angles.
5. Perform the computational-basis projective measurement on the phase register. Its specified Lüders instrument has branch map $Z\mapsto (|y\rangle\langle y|\otimes I_H)Z(|y\rangle\langle y|\otimes I_H)$ for each label $y$ ([[def-qc-projective-measurement]], [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]]). Output the observed label $y$ and the ratio $y/Q$.

The inverse in step 4 is the inverse QFT, not $U^{-1}$; a forward QPE run makes no controlled inverse-unitary query. The coherent prefix is the circuit through step 4 before measurement. A consumer that coherently uncomputes this prefix needs the separate controlled inverse-power capability from [[def-qa-eigenphase-estimation-model]].

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

For an integer $N\ge1$, let $\mathcal F_N$ be the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalized transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]. Define the **cyclic quantum Fourier transform** by $\operatorname{QFT}_N:=\mathcal F_N^{-1}$. The inverse exists by [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]], and its matrix on the standard basis indexed by $0,\ldots,N-1$ is

$$\operatorname{QFT}_N|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ixy/N}|y\rangle,\qquad 0\le x<N.$$

Here the standard-basis ket convention is the one specified by [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. Thus the transform has the positive sign and the same $N^{-1/2}$ normalization as the inverse Fourier formula. At $N=1$ it is the identity on the one-dimensional register. In the binary specialization $N=2^n$, the circuit page writes each index in its unique base-two expansion.

For every $n\ge0$, the exact binary circuit of [[alg-qa-exact-binary-qft-circuit]] implements [[def-qa-cyclic-quantum-fourier-transform]] at $N=2^n$: it maps each computational basis vector $|x\rangle$, $0\le x<2^n$, to

$$2^{-n/2}\sum_{y=0}^{2^n-1}e^{2\pi ixy/2^n}|y\rangle,$$

with the declared output register order. Hence its denotation is $\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}$ on every state. Reversing the gate list and replacing every gate by its adjoint gives the negative-sign inverse QFT with the same ideal gate count.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite projective measurement on $H$. Then $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$ lies in $[0,1]$ for every $a$, and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $E=(e_j)_{j<n}$ and $F=(f_i)_{i<m}$. Let $T:H\to K$ be
linear ([[def-linear-map]]), and write $T_{ij}$ for the $(i,j)$ entry of its
matrix in these bases.
Then, for every $z\in H$,

$$Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}f_i, \qquad T=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}|f_i\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

For $x\in K$ and $y\in H$, the rank-one map $|x\rangle\langle y|$ has
coordinate matrix $[x]_F[y]_E^\dagger$, where $M^\dagger=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$.
Its amplitude satisfies
$\langle x|T|y\rangle_D=\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}$.
All sums are empty when an index dimension is zero, and the identities include
those cases.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Then

$$\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\begin{cases}N,&k\equiv\ell\pmod N,\\\\ 0,&k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N.\end{cases}$$

At $N=1$ the congruence holds for all $k,\ell$ and the sum is $1$. The sum is the finite sum of the complex family $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}$ over the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and $N$ on the right is the natural number $N$ read in $\mathbb C$ as the additive multiple $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$, that is, the value at $N$ of the canonical embedding $\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]).

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

derivations.claim: Before the controlled powers, the state is $Q^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{Q-1}|x\rangle\otimes\psi$ by [F2]. Write $x=\sum_j c_j2^j$, where $c_j$ is the bit at wire $q_{m-1-j}$ by [F1]. The controlled operation on that wire applies $U^{2^j}$ exactly when $c_j=1$; multiplying the eigenvalues gives $\prod_j\exp(2\pi i\theta c_j2^j)=\exp(2\pi i\theta x)$. Hence the state after the controlled-power stage is $Q^{-1/2}\sum_x\exp(2\pi i\theta x)|x\rangle\otimes\psi$. Reading this gate sequence as an operator on the ordered register uses [F9].

The inverse QFT matrix coefficient from input $x$ to output $y$ is $Q^{-1/2}\exp(-2\pi ixy/Q)$, by [F3] and the adjoint convention. Applying it to step 1.1 gives $\chi=\sum_{y=0}^{Q-1}a_y|y\rangle\otimes\psi$, where $a_y=Q^{-1}\sum_{x=0}^{Q-1}\exp(2\pi ix(\theta-y/Q))$. The sign is positive in the eigenphase and negative in the inverse-QFT coefficient, yielding the displayed difference $\theta-y/Q$. The operator ordering is the one in [F9].

The vector $\chi$ is normalized. Indeed, expand the finite squared moduli using [F7] and interchange the finite sums: $\sum_y|a_y|^2=Q^{-2}\sum_{x,x'}\exp(2\pi i(x-x')\theta)\sum_y\exp(-2\pi i(x-x')y/Q)$. By [F6], the inner sum is $Q$ when $x=x'$ and $0$ otherwise, because $0\le x,x'<Q$; therefore $\sum_y|a_y|^2=Q^{-2}Q\cdot Q=1$. Since $\|\psi\|=1$ and the $|y\rangle$ are orthonormal, $\|\chi\|=1$.

The ray-projector theorem [F5] makes $\rho=|\chi\rangle\langle\chi|$ a density operator. The phase-register projective outcome has projector $P_y$ from [F4], so it extracts $a_y|y\rangle\otimes\psi$. By [F5] and [F8], $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_y)=\operatorname{tr}(P_y\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(|P_y\chi\rangle\langle\chi|)=\langle P_y\chi,\chi\rangle_{\rm root}=\|P_y\chi\|^2=|a_y|^2$, where the penultimate equality uses $P_y=P_y^*=P_y^2$. The outcome law in [F4] therefore gives this probability to the classical label $y$. Substituting the value of $a_y$ from step 2.1 gives exactly the displayed $P_\theta(y)$.

The finite sum in the displayed law is defined for every $y,\theta$, including when $Q\theta$ is an integer. For its geometric-sum specialization, the denominator is zero exactly when $z=\exp(2\pi i(\theta-y/Q))=1$, equivalently $Q\theta-y\in Q\mathbb Z$; in every other case [[lem-qa-phase-estimation-geometric-sum]] gives the nonzero-denominator quotient. Thus the stated squared-sum law handles all phases without an undefined quotient.

**Input.** An integer $m\ge1$; an $m$-qubit phase register; a finite-dimensional system register $H$; a unitary $U:H\to H$; a unit eigenvector $\psi$ with promised phase $\theta\in[0,1)$; and one of the forward access capabilities in [[def-qa-eigenphase-estimation-model]].

**Output.** A classical label $y\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$ and its phase estimate $y/Q$, where $Q=2^m$.

**Instructions.**

1. Initialize the phase register in $|0^m\rangle$ and the system register in $\psi$.
2. Apply the Hadamard $H=(X+Z)/\sqrt2$ of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] to each phase wire. This prepares $Q^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{Q-1}|x\rangle\otimes\psi$ in the declared big-endian order.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,m-1$, apply the supplied controlled $U^{2^j}$ to control wire $q_{m-1-j}$ and the system. Under single controlled-unitary access, implement that operation with $2^j$ sequential calls to $C(U)$, as specified by the access model.
4. Apply the inverse of the positive-sign exact binary QFT circuit of [[def-qa-cyclic-quantum-fourier-transform]] and [[thm-qa-exact-binary-qft-circuit-correct]]. Construct it by reversing the chronological gate list and replacing each gate by its adjoint, including the final swaps and negating controlled-phase angles.
5. Perform the computational-basis projective measurement on the phase register. Its specified Lüders instrument has branch map $Z\mapsto (|y\rangle\langle y|\otimes I_H)Z(|y\rangle\langle y|\otimes I_H)$ for each label $y$ ([[def-qc-projective-measurement]], [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]]). Output the observed label $y$ and the ratio $y/Q$.

The inverse in step 4 is the inverse QFT, not $U^{-1}$; a forward QPE run makes no controlled inverse-unitary query. The coherent prefix is the circuit through step 4 before measurement. A consumer that coherently uncomputes this prefix needs the separate controlled inverse-power capability from [[def-qa-eigenphase-estimation-model]].

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

For $n\ge0$, the exact circuit uses $n$ Hadamards, $n(n-1)/2$ controlled phase rotations, $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ SWAP gates, no ancillas, and

$$n+\frac{n(n-1)}2+\lfloor n/2\rfloor=O(n^2)$$

ideal gates in the model of [[def-qa-qft-gate-cost-model]]. If every SWAP is expanded into three exact CNOTs, the circuit instead has $3\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ CNOTs in place of the SWAPs.

Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$ with maximum arity $k:=\max(\{r(g):g\in G\}\cup\{0\})$ and a circuit from [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]]. The declared **size** is the number of gate occurrences, equivalently $\sum_{t=1}^d|L_t|$; the declared **depth** is the number $d$ of explicit layers, not a minimum over alternate layerings; the **width** is the number $n$ of all wires, including workspace wires. The operation model may also assign weighted gate costs, classical bit costs, and query costs; these are separate coordinates and are summed over the calls actually made.

A workspace wire is an ancilla. A **clean-ancilla promise** specifies computational-basis zero states for the ancillas and requires their exact return for every allowed data input: if $U$ is the implemented unitary, $V_D$ is the declared data unitary, and $|0_A\rangle$ is the specified joint zero vector, then $U(x\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V_Dx\otimes|0_A\rangle$ for every allowed data vector $x$. A **dirty-ancilla promise** permits an arbitrary ancilla state independent of the data input; it may be correlated with an untouched reference. Exact dirty-ancilla restoration means the implemented unitary on data and ancillas is $V_D\otimes I_A$ on the entire joint space, where $V_D$ is the declared unitary on data. The same operator equality then holds after tensoring with the identity on any finite untouched reference. Consequently, product input between the data and the combined ancilla/reference system remains product after the operation. No uncorrelated-output claim is made for an initially data-correlated ancilla.

A controlled or inverse operation is counted only when the operation model explicitly grants that access or supplies a construction; its charge is recorded separately from an ordinary call unless the model explicitly combines them. In particular, the matrix of $U$ alone supplies neither a controlled call nor an inverse query, in accordance with [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]] and [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]].

For $n\in\mathbb N$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$S_n(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}z^j,$$
with the empty sum $S_0(z)=0$. Then
$$S_n(z)=\begin{cases}\iota_{\mathbb C}(n),&z=1,\\[2pt](1-z^n)/(1-z),&z\ne1,\end{cases}$$
where $\iota_{\mathbb C}$ is the canonical natural embedding of $\mathbb N$ into $\mathbb C$.

For $Q=2^m$, $\theta\in[0,1)$, and integer $y$, setting
$z=\exp(2\pi i(\theta-y/Q))$ gives
$z^Q=\exp(2\pi iQ\theta)$; moreover $z=1$ exactly when
$Q\theta-y\in Q\mathbb Z$.

derivations.claim: Under controlled-power access, the loop in [F1] invokes exactly one supplied operation for each of the $m$ indices $j=0,\ldots,m-1$, hence exactly $m$ controlled-power queries.

Under single controlled-unitary access, block multiplication gives $C(U)^r=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,U^r)=C(U^r)$ for every natural $r$. Thus the $j$-th controlled power is implemented by $2^j$ calls, so the total is $\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^j=2^m-1=Q-1$ by [F4].

The supplied power circuits contribute $\sum_j C_j$ ordinary gates. Phase-register preparation contributes $m$ Hadamards, and the inverse QFT contributes the count in [F3]. Adding gives the displayed unitary gate count; reversing the QFT circuit changes neither its count nor the query count.

Measurement outputs one $m$-bit label. The operation model [F5] keeps query, ordinary-gate, and classical-bit costs separate; the input eigenstate's preparation is outside the theorem's stated count. Therefore the displayed formula asserts only the stated gate profile and does not infer an implementation of powers from a black-box $U$.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

For a real $x\in[-1,1]$, define its circular distance to the nearest integer by
$$d_{\mathbb T}(x):=\min\{|x|,\,1-|x|\}.$$
Here $|x|$ is the real absolute value and $\min$ is the minimum of the displayed finite set ([[def-real-order]], [[def-max-min]]); existence of this finite minimum follows from [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]. Both entries lie in $[0,1]$, so the value lies in $[0,1/2]$. If $|x|\le1/2$, the nearest integer is $0$; if $x>1/2$, it is $1$; if $x<-1/2$, it is $-1$, so the formula is the distance to the nearest integer. For phases $\theta,\phi\in[0,1)$, their circular distance is $d_{\mathbb T}(\theta-\phi)$; the difference belongs to $(-1,1)$, the stated domain.

Let $m\ge1$, $Q=2^m$, and let the input be an eigenvector with
$U\psi=\exp(2\pi i\theta)\psi$, where $\theta\in[0,1)$.
For each $y\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$, the probability of measuring $y$ in the algorithm of [[alg-qa-quantum-phase-estimation]] is
$$P_\theta(y)=Q^{-2}\left|\sum_{j=0}^{Q-1}\exp\!\left(2\pi i j(\theta-y/Q)\right)\right|^2.$$
Thus the finite outcome kernel is defined at every phase, including $Q\theta\in\mathbb Z$; no quotient with a zero denominator is needed in this formula.

For $n\in\mathbb N$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$S_n(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}z^j,$$
with the empty sum $S_0(z)=0$. Then
$$S_n(z)=\begin{cases}\iota_{\mathbb C}(n),&z=1,\\[2pt](1-z^n)/(1-z),&z\ne1,\end{cases}$$
where $\iota_{\mathbb C}$ is the canonical natural embedding of $\mathbb N$ into $\mathbb C$.

For $Q=2^m$, $\theta\in[0,1)$, and integer $y$, setting
$z=\exp(2\pi i(\theta-y/Q))$ gives
$z^Q=\exp(2\pi iQ\theta)$; moreover $z=1$ exactly when
$Q\theta-y\in Q\mathbb Z$.

For $0\le u\le1/2$ and $v\ge0$,
$$\sin(\pi u)\ge2u,\qquad \sin(v)\le v.$$

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
